row.title: The screen never says stop
row.evidence_anchor: Young children find it harder to move on from a tablet than from a book, and routines and natural stopping points make the move easier than a countdown
statutory_hooks: EfCW health, wellbeing and lifestyle, early years to 7
row.single_action_outcome: I can pick a stop and wave bye bye to the screen.

slides.caption: Follow the star. In as it grows, out as it shrinks.
slides.script: Before we meet Pebble, we settle. Sit on the carpet with hands on tummies. Say: this is our star breath, we do it at the start of every screen lesson. Watch the star grow and breathe in with it, watch it shrink and breathe out. Four together without talking. If a child cannot sit still, they can do it standing with arms rising and falling, that counts too.

slides.title: The screen never says stop
slides.script: Read the title slowly and let it hang for a second. Then say: screens are lovely, and screens are very good at keeping going. Today Pebble has a problem with that, and we are going to help. By home time every one of you will know a way to stop a screen without a big fight, and you will be able to teach it to your grown ups tonight.

slides.heading: Pebble is here!
lines: My cartoon ended. Then another one started all by itself!
I did not know how to stop. Can you help me?
slides.script: Let Pebble land and say the lines. Read Pebble's question once in your own voice and leave it hanging, with a shrug: how do you stop a screen that keeps going? Do not answer it yet. Say: Pebble needs us. Let us find out what today is for.

slides.outcome: I can pick a stop and wave bye bye to the screen.
slides.why: Screens keep going, so we choose when to stop.
gains: Find the stop in a song, a show or a game
Wave bye bye to the screen
Go to a good next thing
slides.script: Read the I can sentence together, twice, with a wave on the words bye bye. Then say the why in your own words: nobody is in trouble for loving a screen. Screens are made to keep going, so the stop has to come from us. Point at each of the three things we will learn, and do the actions: a flat hand for stop, a wave, and marching arms for the next thing.

slides.prompt: Tell your partner a good thing to do after screens.
slides.lookFor: Play, dinner, bath, a story, the park. Every answer counts.
slides.script: Give ten seconds of thinking time first, fingers on lips. Then one minute with a talk partner. Listen out for lovely next things: the park, Lego, a bath with bubbles, a story with Grandad. Take four or five and say each one back warmly. Keep a list on the board, because we come back to it: these are our next things, and a good next thing is what makes stopping easier.

slides.heading: Our three words today

words.meaning: The end of a bit, like the end of a song.
What we say to the screen when it is time.
Something good to do after the screen goes off.

slides.script: Say each word with its action and have the class echo it. Stop: a flat hand held up. Bye bye: a big wave. Next thing: marching arms, off we go. Do all three in a row twice, then once more quietly. Land the first one: a stop is just the end of a bit, like the end of a song, and nobody is in trouble at a stop.

slides.question: A picture on a screen might be pretend. What do we do?

options.text: Stop, look, ask a grown up
options.feedback: That is Pebble's tool from our first lesson. We stop, we look carefully, and a grown up helps us find out what is real.

options.text: Believe it straight away because we can see it
options.feedback: Seeing it on a screen does not make it real. A computer can make pictures of things that never happened, so we stop, look and ask.
A secret leaves us alone with the puzzle. Asking a grown up is how we find out, and we are never in trouble for asking.

slides.script: This is our remembering question from the first lesson with Pebble. Thinking time first, count to five in your heads. Then everyone votes with fingers: one, two or three. Take one answer with a reason. Then bridge to today: last time the word stop helped us with what is real. Today the word stop helps us with screens that keep going.

slides.heading: Screens keep going
slides.body: One ends. The next one starts by itself.
slides.script: Here is what I notice first when I watch cartoons on a tablet: when one ends, I do not get a moment to choose. The next one is already starting. Nobody pressed anything. Show it with your hands: one cartoon ends, clap, and the next one pops up straight away. Say plainly: the screen is made to keep going, because the people who make it want you to keep watching. Nobody did anything wrong. It just means the screen will not tell you when to stop, so the stop has to come from somewhere else.

slides.question: Pebble's cartoon ends. What happens next on most screens?

options.feedback: On most screens the next cartoon starts all by itself, without anybody choosing it. That is why the stop has to come from us.

options.text: The screen says it is time for bed now
options.feedback: Screens hardly ever say that. The screen will not tell you when to stop, because it starts the next one by itself.
It would be handy if it did. Most screens keep going instead, and the next cartoon starts all by itself.

slides.script: Wait five seconds before anyone answers. Then everyone shows fingers, one, two or three. The popular wrong answer is the second one, because it is what children wish would happen. Read its reason out: the screen will not tell you when to stop, it starts the next one by itself. Ask: so if the screen does not stop, who does? Take the big answer: we do.

slides.heading: Every show has a stop
slides.body: A song ends. A story ends.
slides.script: Teach the idea of a stop as the end of a bit, not a punishment. Sing the first line of a song the class knows and stop at the end: that is a stop. Open a picture book to the last page and close it: that is a stop. A race in a game has a finish line: that is a stop. Say: every show, song and game has little stops inside it. Grown ups and children who are good at screens look for the stop, because stopping at a stop feels much easier than stopping in the middle.

slides.prompt: Where is the stop in Pebble's cartoon? Tell your partner.
slides.lookFor: The end, the music at the end, the words the end.
slides.script: Thinking time first, count to five quietly. Then a minute in pairs. Help pairs who are stuck: what happens at the end of a cartoon? The music plays, the words come up, the characters wave. Every ending counts. Take three answers and say: yes, that is the stop. That is the moment to wave bye bye, before the next one starts by itself.

slides.heading: Pick a stop
slides.caption: Then the screen can rest.

steps.title: Pick a stop
steps.text: Before you start, choose: one show, one song.

steps.title: Wave bye bye
steps.text: At the stop, wave to the screen.

steps.title: Go to the next thing
steps.text: Play, dinner, a bath or a story.

slides.script: This is Pebble's tool, so take your time. Point to each step as it appears and do its action with the class. The first one is the clever part: the stop is picked before the screen goes on, with a grown up, so nobody has to argue about it later. Here is what I would do at home: I would say one cartoon, then bath, before I press play. Then the second step: when the stop comes, a big wave to the screen. Then the third: march off to the next thing from our list on the board. Chant the three steps with actions, three times, getting louder. Then point at the three chips at the bottom: a stop, not yet, or ask a grown up. We will use them in our game after half time.

slides.question: The race in Pebble's game is finished. What now?

options.text: Wave bye bye, then the next thing
options.feedback: The end of the race is a stop. Pebble waves bye bye to the screen and goes to the next thing on the list.

options.text: Start one more race, then one more after that
options.feedback: One more and one more is how the screen keeps going. The end of a race is a stop, so it is time to wave bye bye.

options.text: Hide so nobody can say stop
options.feedback: Hiding means nobody can help Pebble with a big feeling. The finish line is a stop, so Pebble waves bye bye and moves on.

slides.script: Thinking time, five seconds, then everyone votes with fingers. The popular wrong answer is one more race, because it feels fair and fun. Say it kindly: one more is exactly what the screen wants, and one more always turns into one more after that. The finish line is a stop. Do the tool together once: pick a stop, wave bye bye, go to the next thing.

slides.heading: A grumpy bye bye is fine
slides.body: Big breath, then on we go.
slides.script: Say this warmly and slowly. Sometimes when we wave bye bye to a screen, a grumpy feeling arrives. That is fine. Grown ups feel it too when they put their phones down. A grumpy feeling is allowed. It means your body liked the screen. So we do DiGi Junior's star breath, one big breath in and out, and then we go to our next thing. Show the class: make a grumpy face, take one star breath, then march off to the next thing. The grumpy bye bye still counts as a bye bye.

config.heading: Half time! Everyone together
config.prompt: Breathe in as Pebble grows, out as Pebble shrinks. Then stand up and wave bye bye to the board.

slides.script: Half time. Two breaths with the whole room, in as Pebble grows and out as Pebble shrinks. Then everyone stands up and gives the board the biggest wave bye bye they can. Then sit down, ready for the game.

slides.caption: A stop, not yet, or ask a grown up?

config.label: A stop, or not yet? · tap the class answer

posts.text: The song has finished and the music has stopped.
posts.why: The end of a song is a stop. Wave bye bye.

posts.text: Pebble's race is only half done.
posts.why: Halfway is not a stop yet. Finish the race, then stop.

posts.text: The cartoon ended, and a new one is starting by itself.
posts.why: The end was the stop. The new one is the screen keeping going.

posts.text: Your grown up says it is time for dinner.
posts.why: When your grown up says stop, that is a stop too.

posts.text: The game says: pay for more lives?
posts.why: Anything that wants money is a job for your grown up.

posts.text: You cannot find a stop anywhere in this game.
posts.why: Some games have no stop. Ask your grown up to help pick one.

config.doneBody: A stop, not yet, and the ones to ask about.

slides.script: We play it together before we try it with our bodies. Tap the first card and read it out with plenty of drama. Hands up for each of the three answers, then tap the one the class chose and read the reason. Do all six. Two cards matter most. The dinner card: when a grown up says stop, that is a stop too, even in the middle. And the tricky game: some games are built with no stop at all, so the answer is to ask a grown up to help pick one before playing. If the class picks wrong, read the reason and ask what they think now.

slides.label: Your turn
slides.heading: Play screen and stopper
slides.body: Find the stop. Wave bye bye.
slides.script: A game in pairs. One child is the screen: they sing a short song they know, and when it ends they say in a big screen voice, and here comes another one! The other child is the stopper: they listen for the end of the song, hold up a flat hand, wave bye bye to the screen, and say their next thing out loud, for example: bye bye screen, now I am going to play Lego. Swap after each go. Model it once first with a child as the screen and you as the stopper. Circulate and catch pairs who stop at the end of the song rather than the middle, and name it: you found the stop. Finish with everyone drawing their next thing on the sheet, the thing they will do tonight after screens.

slides.question: Pebble picked one show. The show has ended. What now?

options.text: Wave bye bye, then the next thing
options.feedback: Pebble picked one show, and the end of it is the stop. Pebble waves bye bye and goes to the next thing.

options.text: Just one more, and then one more after
options.feedback: The stop was picked before the show began. One more is the screen keeping going, so Pebble waves bye bye instead.

options.text: Shout at the screen until it goes away
options.feedback: Shouting makes a big feeling bigger. A star breath and a wave bye bye are how Pebble gets to the next thing.

slides.script: First of our two finishing questions, and every child answers. Read the question and all three answers aloud with actions, wait five seconds, then everyone votes with fingers. Ask one child to show the wave and say the next thing. Record who got it on the exit sheet by eye; nobody's answer is read out as wrong.

slides.question: Your grown up says stop in the middle. What then?

options.text: Keep going until the very end
options.feedback: It is hard to stop in the middle. But when a grown up says stop, that is a stop too, so we wave bye bye.

options.text: Stop, because a grown up's stop counts too
options.feedback: A grown up's stop is a real stop, even in the middle. Take a star breath, wave bye bye, and go to the next thing.

options.text: Hide the tablet under a cushion
options.feedback: Hiding the tablet means the grumpy feeling stays. When a grown up says stop, we wave bye bye and go to the next thing.

slides.script: Second finishing question, same routine: read it with feeling, thinking time of five seconds, then fingers. This is the one grown ups at home will care about most, so land it: a grown up's stop counts too, even in the middle, and a grumpy bye bye is still a bye bye. If a child says their grown up gets cross about screens, thank them for telling you and say that is why we are practising, so stopping gets easier for everyone.

slides.label: Say it like Pebble
slides.text: Pick a stop. Wave bye bye. Off to the next thing!
slides.script: Pebble's chant, all together with the actions: flat hand, big wave, marching arms. Three times: a whisper, a talking voice, then big and proud. This is the sentence you want them saying to their grown ups at home time.

slides.heading: What we know now
points: Screens keep going. The next one starts by itself.
So we pick a stop before we start.
At the stop, we wave bye bye.
Then off we go to the next thing.
slides.script: Read the four points together, with the actions on the last three. Then ask: who picks the stop, the screen or us? Wait for the big answer: us. That is the answer going home in every book bag.

slides.heading: Pebble's job for you
lines: Tonight, pick your stop before the screen goes on.
At the stop, wave bye bye.
Then tell your grown up your next thing!
slides.script: The handover. Say nothing over it. When the last line lands, ask them to look at you and say the job once more in their own words. The passport is next, then DiGi Junior says goodbye.

config.heading: The passport
config.prompt: Today filled a little bit of the First steps page. Tap to fill it in!
config.after: A full page brings the big check, and the big check earns Pebble's stamp!

slides.script: DiGi Junior keeps a special book called the passport, the book of getting ready for screens all the way to sixteen. Every lesson fills a little bit of the page, and jobs at home fill it too. Ask one child to tap Fill the page, and when the ring moves, everybody shouts stamp. Nobody can fail the passport, it only ever fills up. The note going home tells your grown ups which page it is. The count on the wall is this screen's memory of your class, not any child's record.

slides.heading: DiGi Junior says goodbye
lines: Star pause with me! Arms out wide, breathe in, and out.
Screens keep going, so you pick the stop.
Wave bye bye, then off to your next thing.
See you next time, little stars! ⭐
slides.script: Let DiGi Junior land the ending; read each bubble aloud in your best DiGi Junior voice, because most of the class cannot read them yet. Do the star pause with the class on the first line. Send the parent note home in book bags today, so families hear the chant tonight. Wave goodbye to DiGi Junior with twinkling star fingers, which is also the last bye bye of the day.

parent_note.headline: What we taught today, and one thing to try at home
parent_note.taught: Today your child learned that most screens never say stop: when one cartoon ends, the next one starts by itself. So we pick the stop together before the screen goes on (one show, one song, one race), and at the stop we wave bye bye and go to a good next thing. They also learned that when a grown up says stop, that is a stop too, and that a grumpy bye bye is fine.
parent_note.try_this: Before the screen goes on tonight, agree the stop out loud together: one episode, then bath. When the episode ends, wave bye bye to the screen with them and go straight to the next thing you agreed. Researchers who asked families about this found that stopping at a natural end and having a routine made it easier than a countdown warning.
parent_note.family_question: What is our stop tonight, and what is your next thing after it?
parent_note.passport: Today also filled a little of your child's passport page. The passport is the journey to sixteen that home and school walk together: lessons fill it at school, jobs and little wins fill it at home, and each stage of growing up ends with a stamp. Ask your child to show you Pebble's wave.

teacher_notes.learning_objective: Pupils understand that most screens keep going on their own, and practise a simple routine for ending screen time: pick a stop before starting, wave bye bye at the stop, and go to a good next thing.
teacher_notes.essential_question: If the screen never says stop, who does?
teacher_notes.timing: 47 minutes: connect 3, starter 9, cycle one 8, cycle two 8, practise 10, prove 4, close 5

cycles.title: Screens keep going
cycles.outcome: I can say that the next show often starts by itself.

cycles.title: Pick a stop
cycles.outcome: I can pick a stop, wave bye bye and go to my next thing.

tool.heading: Pick a stop
tool.strapline: The screen keeps going, so I choose the stop.

keywords.definition: The end of a bit, like the end of a song, a story or a race.
What we say and wave to the screen when the stop comes.
Something good to do after the screen goes off, picked before it goes on.

prior_knowledge: From eyfs-01, Screens and kindness: stop, look, ask a grown up, and that we are never in trouble for asking.
Children can name some screen things they love: cartoons, songs, games on a tablet.
Children know the end of a song or a story when they hear it.
key_learning_points: Most screens keep going on their own: the next cartoon starts by itself.
Every show, song and game has stops inside it, like the end of a song.
We pick the stop with a grown up before the screen goes on.
At the stop we wave bye bye and go to a good next thing.
A grown up's stop counts too, and a grumpy bye bye is fine.
misconceptions: That the screen will tell you when to stop. It will not: most screens start the next one by itself, so the stop is chosen by us.
That stopping is a punishment. A stop is the end of a bit, like the end of a song, and the next thing is something good.
That a grumpy feeling at the stop means you did it wrong. Grumpy is normal, a star breath helps, and the bye bye still counts.
i_can: I can say that the next show often starts by itself.
I can pick a stop, wave bye bye and go to my next thing.
teacher_notes.commitment_stem: My commitment: tonight my stop is ... and my next thing is ...
teacher_notes.teacher_tip: Model the stop yourself at least once today with something real: end a song on the class speaker at its natural end, wave bye bye to it, and say your next thing out loud. Children copy the routine far faster than they learn the rule, and a class that has seen an adult do a calm bye bye will do one at home.
teacher_notes.equipment: The board with sound for the star breath. A short song the class knows for the screen and stopper game. The drawing sheet and crayons.
teacher_notes.paper_fallback: The whole lesson runs without the board. Draw the three steps as three boxes with a hand, a wave and a train, sing the song for the stop game, read the six sort cards aloud with hands up for each answer, and read the two finishing questions with fingers for the votes.

differentiation.support: Pair the three words with their three actions every single time they come up, and let children answer with the action instead of words. In the stopper game, partner a child with an adult first so they hear a clear song ending before they try with a friend.
differentiation.stretch: Ask stretch children to find the stop in three different things (a song, a book, a game), and to tell you which is hardest to stop and why. Then ask them to pick a stop for a game that has no clear ending.

send.eal: Teach stop, bye bye and next thing with the actions and a picture card for each before the lesson. The whole tool can be done with gestures, and the worksheet is a drawing, so no written English is needed to succeed.
send.sensory: Keep the star breath slide ready to revisit at any point. Some children find a sudden ending distressing, so let them practise the wave at a stop they choose, and give a clear visual of the next thing rather than a spoken one.
send.attention: Move bodies between each part: stand for the chant, wave for the bye bye, march for the next thing. The screen and stopper game can be shortened to one round each way without losing the point.
send.communication: Accept the flat hand, the wave and a point at the next thing picture as full answers. A child who cannot say bye bye can wave it, and a child who cannot draw the next thing can choose a picture card.

worksheet.title: Find the stop
worksheet.directions: Your teacher reads each one aloud. Circle: a stop, not yet, or ask a grown up. Then draw your next thing.

worksheet_items.item: The song has finished and the music has stopped.
worksheet_items.teaching_point: Recognise: the end of a song is the clearest stop there is. This builds the idea of a natural stopping point.

worksheet_items.item: Pebble's race in the game is only half done.
worksheet_items.teaching_point: Recognise: the middle is not a stop. Finishing the bit and then stopping is easier than stopping in the middle.

worksheet_items.item: The cartoon ended, and a new one is starting all by itself.
worksheet_items.teaching_point: Apply: the end was the stop, and the next one starting is the screen keeping going. The key idea of the lesson.

worksheet_items.item: Your grown up says it is time for dinner, and the show is in the middle.
worksheet_items.teaching_point: Apply: a grown up's stop counts too. The routine includes stopping when the grown up says so, not only at the end.

worksheet_items.item: The game says: pay for more lives?
worksheet_items.teaching_point: Apply: anything that asks for money is a job for a grown up. This seeds the next lesson, paws off and ask first.

worksheet_items.item: You cannot find a stop anywhere in this game.
worksheet_items.teaching_point: Explain: some games are built with no natural end. The grown up helps pick one before the game starts.

starter_quiz.question: What are Pebble's three words from our first lesson?
starter_quiz.answer: Stop, look, ask a grown up.
starter_quiz.teaching_point: Carried forward from eyfs-01. The word stop comes back today with a new job.

starter_quiz.question: Which one is a real end?
options: The last page of a book
starter_quiz.answer: The last page of a book
starter_quiz.teaching_point: Children already know endings from books and songs. The lesson builds on that.

starter_quiz.question: If something on a screen makes you feel funny, you should keep it a secret.
starter_quiz.teaching_point: Carried forward from eyfs-01. Telling a grown up is always the move, and it is never trouble.

starter_quiz.question: Name one thing you love to do that is not a screen.
starter_quiz.answer: Any real activity, such as the park, Lego, a bath, a story.
starter_quiz.teaching_point: This becomes the child's next thing. A child with no answer needs one found before the lesson ends.

exit_quiz.question: When one cartoon ends, the next one often starts by itself.
exit_quiz.teaching_point: The mechanism in one line. The screen keeps going, so the stop comes from us.

exit_quiz.question: What are Pebble's three steps?
exit_quiz.answer: Pick a stop, wave bye bye, go to the next thing.
exit_quiz.teaching_point: The portable routine. If it does not come back, chant it together twice before home time.

exit_quiz.question: Which one is a stop?
exit_quiz.teaching_point: A stop is the end of a bit. The new cartoon starting is the screen keeping going.

exit_quiz.question: When a grown up says stop, that is a stop too.
exit_quiz.teaching_point: The part families care about most. A grown up's stop counts, even in the middle.

evidence_base.claim: Toddlers showed more difficulty moving away from a tablet than from a print book, including more tantrums, in a laboratory comparison.
evidence_base.source: Munzer, Miller, Wang, Kaciroti and Radesky (2021), Tablets, toddlers and tantrums: the immediate effects of tablet device play, Acta Paediatrica 110, 255 to 256
evidence_base.status: Read through the publisher's abstract and a search extract on 30 September 2026; the full paper was not reachable from the build container. Used for the direction only. The children were toddlers, younger than Reception, and no figure from it appears on a slide.

evidence_base.claim: In interviews with 27 parents and a diary study with 28 families of toddlers and preschoolers, routines and disengaging at a natural stopping point made the move away from technology easier, and a two minute warning was not associated with easier transitions.
evidence_base.source: Hiniker, Suh, Cao and Kientz (2016), Screen Time Tantrums: How Families Manage Screen Media Experiences for Toddlers and Preschoolers, CHI 2016
evidence_base.status: Read through the university's release and search extracts on 30 September 2026. A diary study, so it shows association, not cause. It is why the lesson teaches the end of a bit rather than a countdown, and why the parent note says what researchers found rather than a rule.

evidence_base.claim: Features such as autoplay, rewards, progress structures and characters are built into children's digital options to sustain engagement, and when an activity is highly engaging young children find it harder to disengage.
evidence_base.source: Young children's ability to disengage from program viewing vs. app play and the role of self regulation, International Journal of Child Computer Interaction, 2026
evidence_base.status: Read through a search extract of the abstract on 30 September 2026. Used only for the teacher's explanation that the screen is made to keep going; nothing on a slide depends on it.

evidence_base.claim: Education for a Connected World sets out, for early years to age 7, that a child can identify rules that help keep us safe and healthy in and beyond the home when using technology.
evidence_base.source: UK Council for Internet Safety, Education for a Connected World, 2020 edition, Health, wellbeing and lifestyle strand
evidence_base.status: The wording was confirmed through a search extract of the framework on 30 September 2026; gov.uk was blocked from the build container.

hard_questions.question: What if my grown up lets me keep watching?
hard_questions.answer: Then that is your grown up's choice, and that is fine. Every family picks its own stops. What we learned today is how to stop when it is time, whenever that is, without a big fight.

hard_questions.question: Why does the next one start by itself?
hard_questions.answer: Because the people who make the app want you to keep watching, so they made it start the next one for you. That is why the stop has to come from us, not the screen.

hard_questions.question: What if I get really cross when it stops?
hard_questions.answer: That happens to lots of people, grown ups too. Cross is just a feeling. Take a star breath, wave bye bye even if it is a grumpy wave, and go to your next thing. The cross feeling gets smaller.

hard_questions.question: Are screens bad?
hard_questions.answer: No. Screens can be fun, and we can learn from them. We are learning how to stop them, so we are the ones in charge and not the screen.

parent_questions.question: Should I give a five minute warning?
parent_questions.answer: A warning on its own did not make stopping easier in the one study of families we know of. What helped was agreeing the stop before starting and stopping at a natural end, like the end of an episode, with a clear next thing to go to.

parent_questions.question: My child has a meltdown whenever the tablet goes off. Is that normal?
parent_questions.answer: It is very common, and researchers have seen more upset when toddlers move away from a tablet than from a book. It does not mean anything is wrong. Pick the stop before, stop at an ending, and have the next thing ready. The lesson gives your child the same words you can use.

subject_knowledge.heading: Why the stop is picked before the screen goes on
subject_knowledge.body: Stopping in the middle of something engaging is hard at any age, and harder at four. The research on families with young children found that routines and stopping at a natural end helped, while a warning with no agreed end did not. So the tool puts the decision before the screen is on, when nobody is in the middle of anything, and makes the stop an ending the child can hear, like the end of an episode. The next thing gives the child somewhere to go, which is why the lesson starts by listing good next things.

subject_knowledge.heading: Why the lesson says the screen is made to keep going
subject_knowledge.body: Autoplay, rewards and characters are designed to keep children watching and playing. Saying so plainly takes the blame off the child: the difficulty of stopping comes from how the product is built, and the child hears that said out loud. That framing matters at four, because a child who believes stopping is hard because they are naughty will hide from the stop rather than practise it.

dsl_note.note: This lesson is about ending screen time and carries no disclosure prompt. A child may describe conflict at home around screens, a grown up who shouts, or screens used for very long periods. Most of this is ordinary family life and should be met warmly. If what a child describes suggests neglect or harm, follow your school safeguarding policy and log it on the school concern form the same day.
